title: I Quit Teaching Pt2
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In the second part of his story, Dave Stuart Jr. describes how he stopped drifting and committed to teaching. Hired as a long-term sub at $75 a day into a faculty steeped in professional literature he had never read, he was mostly failing, and was still weighing seminary, publishing and a return to coffee-shop work. A night in a seminary student center made it clear that those were not his people, and he reasoned his way to a decision using three components of calling: affinity, ability and a clear need. The post argues that deciding fully, rather than keeping every mountain in view, was the first breakthrough that made all later growth possible. It closes by pointing to the next question, which is what the right questions are.
points: Commitment to one career path, not talent, was the precondition for every later improvement in his practice.
He tests calling with three components: affinity, ability, and a clear need others have.
Being a decent but not great teacher was enough, because the belief that he could improve was the real qualification.
Surrounding himself with people reading and debating the craft revealed what he wanted to join.
quotes: My approach to classroom management, which had become quite effective in Baltimore, was making a real mess of things now. It seemed like a new kid was mad at me every day.
I realized that I wanted to get better, and I liked the thought of that pursuit.
I had an ability for it: I wasn’t anywhere near a great teacher, but I was a decent one. I couldn’t be the worst one. And I was certain of this: I could improve.
No more sitting at the bottom of a bunch of mountains, torturously fretting about which one to pick. Just, “Okay — teaching. Let’s do teaching, but for real this time. No quitting. All in.
I had decided. That was the first breakthrough — the one without which none of the others would have come.
I sensed, rather than had any studies or literature or research to prove, that school was important, and that it could be better, but that it’d only be better if more people stuck to it long-term.
